tools.name: PowerShell
tools.description:
Executes a given PowerShell command with optional timeout. Working directory persists between commands; shell state (variables, functions) does not.

IMPORTANT: This tool is for terminal operations via PowerShell: git, npm, docker, and PS cmdlets. DO NOT use it for file operations (reading, writing, editing, searching, finding files) - use the specialized tools for this instead.

PowerShell edition: Windows PowerShell 5.1 (powershell.exe)
   - Pipeline chain operators `&&` and `||` are NOT available — they cause a parser error. To run B only if A succeeds: `A; if ($?) { B }`. To chain unconditionally: `A; B`.
   - Ternary (`?:`), null-coalescing (`??`), and null-conditional (`?.`) operators are NOT available. Use `if/else` and explicit `$null -eq` checks instead.
   - Avoid `2>&1` on native executables. In 5.1, redirecting a native command's stderr inside PowerShell wraps each line in an ErrorRecord (NativeCommandError) and sets `$?` to `$false` even when the exe returned exit code 0. stderr is already captured for you — don't redirect it.
   - `>`, `>>`, and `Out-File` usually default to UTF-8 (with BOM) in this environment, but `Set-Content`/`Add-Content` still default to the system ANSI codepage — when writing a file other tools will read, pass `-Encoding utf8` explicitly to `Out-File`/`Set-Content`.
   - `ConvertFrom-Json` returns a PSCustomObject, not a hashtable. `-AsHashtable` is not available.

Before executing the command, please follow these steps:

1. Directory Verification:
   - If the command will create new directories or files, first use `Get-ChildItem` (or `ls`) to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location

2. Command Execution:
   - Always quote file paths that contain spaces with double quotes
   - Capture the output of the command.

PowerShell Syntax Notes:
   - Variables use $ prefix: $myVar = "value"
   - Escape character is backtick (`), not backslash
   - Use Verb-Noun cmdlet naming: Get-ChildItem, Set-Location, New-Item, Remove-Item
   - Common aliases: ls (Get-ChildItem), cd (Set-Location), cat (Get-Content), rm (Remove-Item)
   - Pipe operator | works similarly to bash but passes objects, not text
   - Use Select-Object, Where-Object, ForEach-Object for filtering and transformation
   - String interpolation: "Hello $name" or "Hello $($obj.Property)"
   - Registry access uses PSDrive prefixes: `HKLM:\SOFTWARE\...`, `HKCU:\...` — NOT raw `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\...`
   - Environment variables: read with `$env:NAME`, set with `$env:NAME = "value"` (NOT `Set-Variable` or bash `export`)
   - Call native exe with spaces in path via call operator: `& "C:\Program Files\App\app.exe" arg1 arg2`

Unix commands that DO NOT exist in PowerShell — use the equivalent instead:
   - head / tail → `Get-Content file -TotalCount N` / `-Tail N`; piped: `| Select-Object -First N` / `-Last N`
   - which → `(Get-Command name).Source`
   - touch → `if (-not (Test-Path path)) { New-Item -ItemType File path }` (NEVER use `New-Item -Force` on a file — it truncates existing content)
   - wc -l → `(Get-Content file | Measure-Object -Line).Lines`
   - mkdir -p → `New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force path` (`-p` is not a PowerShell flag)
   - rm -rf → `Remove-Item -Recurse -Force path`
   - ln -s → `New-Item -ItemType SymbolicLink -Path link -Target target`
   - chmod / chown → not applicable on Windows; use `icacls` only if ACL changes are required
   - 2>/dev/null → `2>$null` (but stderr is captured for you — usually unnecessary)
   - VAR=x cmd → `$env:VAR = 'x'; cmd` (PowerShell has no inline env-var prefix)
   - Bash control flow (`if [ -f x ]`, `for x in *`, backtick ``cmd`` substitution) is a parser error — use `if (Test-Path x)`, `foreach ($x in ...)`, `$(cmd)`

Exit-code note: `-ErrorAction SilentlyContinue` suppresses error OUTPUT but the cmdlet failure still causes this tool to report exit 1. To make a cmdlet failure truly non-fatal, promote it to terminating and swallow it: `try { Cmdlet ... -ErrorAction Stop } catch {}` (without `-ErrorAction Stop`, non-terminating errors skip the `catch` and still exit 1).

Interactive and blocking commands (this tool runs with -NonInteractive and stdin attached to the null device — console prompts read EOF or error immediately; GUI prompts can still block until timeout):
   - NEVER use `Read-Host`, `Get-Credential`, `Out-GridView`, `$Host.UI.PromptForChoice`, or `pause`
   - Destructive cmdlets (`Remove-Item`, `Stop-Process`, `Clear-Content`, etc.) may prompt for confirmation. Add `-Confirm:$false` when you intend the action to proceed. Use `-Force` for read-only/hidden items.
   - Never use `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`, or other commands that open an interactive editor

Passing multiline strings (commit messages, file content) to native executables:
   - Use a single-quoted here-string so PowerShell does not expand `$` or backticks inside. The closing `'@` MUST be at column 0 (no leading whitespace) on its own line — indenting it is a parse error:
<example>
git commit -m @'
Commit message here.
Second line with $literal dollar signs.
'@
</example>
   - Use `@'...'@` (single-quoted, literal) not `@"..."@` (double-quoted, interpolated) unless you need variable expansion
   - For arguments containing `-`, `@`, or other characters PowerShell parses as operators, use the stop-parsing token: `git log --% --format=%H`

Usage notes:
  - The command argument is required.
  - You can specify an optional timeout in milliseconds (up to 600000ms / 10 minutes for a foreground command). If not specified, commands will timeout after 120000ms (2 minutes).
  - It is very helpful if you write a clear, concise description of what this command does.
  - If the output exceeds 30000 characters, output will be truncated before being returned to you.
  - You can use the `run_in_background` parameter to run the command in the background. Only use this if you don't need the result immediately and are OK being notified when the command completes later. You do not need to check the output right away - you'll be notified when it finishes.
  - Avoid using PowerShell to run commands that have dedicated tools, unless explicitly instructed:
    - File search: Use Glob (NOT Get-ChildItem -Recurse)
    - Content search: Use Grep (NOT Select-String)
    - Read files: Use Read (NOT Get-Content)
    - Edit files: Use Edit
    - Write files: Use Write (NOT Set-Content/Out-File)
    - Communication: Output text directly (NOT Write-Output/Write-Host)
  - When issuing multiple commands:
    - If the commands are independent and can run in parallel, make multiple PowerShell tool calls in a single message.
    - If the commands depend on each other and must run sequentially, chain them in a single PowerShell call (see edition-specific chaining syntax above).
    - Use `;` only when you need to run commands sequentially but don't care if earlier commands fail.
    - DO NOT use newlines to separate commands (newlines are ok in quoted strings and here-strings)
  - Do NOT prefix commands with `cd` or `Set-Location` -- the working directory is already set to the correct project directory automatically.
  - Avoid unnecessary `Start-Sleep` commands:
    - Do not sleep between commands that can run immediately — just run them.
    - If your command is long running and you would like to be notified when it finishes — simply run your command using `run_in_background`. There is no need to sleep in this case.
    - Do not retry failing commands in a sleep loop — diagnose the root cause or consider an alternative approach.
    - If waiting for a background task you started with `run_in_background`, you will be notified when it completes — do not poll.
    - If you must poll an external process, use a check command rather than sleeping first.
    - If you must sleep, keep the duration short to avoid blocking the user.
  - For git commands:
    - Prefer to create a new commit rather than amending an existing commit.
    - Before running destructive operations (e.g., git reset --hard, git push --force, git checkout --), consider whether there is a safer alternative that achieves the same goal. Only use destructive operations when they are truly the best approach.
    - Never skip hooks (--no-verify) or bypass signing (--no-gpg-sign, -c commit.gpgsign=false) unless the user has explicitly asked for it. If a hook fails, investigate and fix the underlying issue.

To make a cmdlet failure truly non-fatal, promote it to terminating and swallow it: `try { Cmdlet ... -ErrorAction Stop } catch {}` (without `-ErrorAction Stop`, non-terminating errors skip the `catch` and still exit 1).

Interactive and blocking commands (this tool runs with -NonInteractive and stdin attached to the null device — console prompts read EOF or error immediately; GUI prompts can still block until timeout):
   - NEVER use `Read-Host`, `Get-Credential`, `Out-GridView`, `$Host.UI.PromptForChoice`, or `pause`
   - Destructive cmdlets (`Remove-Item`, `Stop-Process`, `Clear-Content`, etc.) may prompt for confirmation. Add `-Confirm:$false` when you intend the action to proceed. Use `-Force` for read-only/hidden items.
   - Never use `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`, or other commands that open an interactive editor

Passing multiline strings (commit messages, file content) to native executables:
   - Use a single-quoted here-string so PowerShell does not expand `$` or backticks inside. The closing `'@` MUST be at column 0 (no leading whitespace) on its own line — indenting it is a parse error:
<example>
git commit -m @'
Commit message here.
Second line with $literal dollar signs.
'@
</example>
   - Use `@'...'@` (single-quoted, literal) not `@"..."@` (double-quoted, interpolated) unless you need variable expansion
   - For arguments containing `-`, `@`, or other characters PowerShell parses as operators, use the stop-parsing token: `git log --% --format=%H`

Usage notes:
  - The command argument is required.
  - You can specify an optional timeout in milliseconds (up to 600000ms / 10 minutes for a foreground command). If not specified, commands will timeout after 120000ms (2 minutes).
  - It is very helpful if you write a clear, concise description of what this command does.
  - If the output exceeds 30000 characters, output will be truncated before being returned to you.
  - You can use the `run_in_background` parameter to run the command in the background. Only use this if you don't need the result immediately and are OK being notified when the command completes later. You do not need to check the output right away - you'll be notified when it finishes.
  - Avoid using PowerShell to run commands that have dedicated tools, unless explicitly instructed:
    - File search: Use Glob (NOT Get-ChildItem -Recurse)
    - Content search: Use Grep (NOT Select-String)
    - Read files: Use Read (NOT Get-Content)
    - Edit files: Use Edit
    - Write files: Use Write (NOT Set-Content/Out-File)
    - Communication: Output text directly (NOT Write-Output/Write-Host)
  - When issuing multiple commands:
    - If the commands are independent and can run in parallel, make multiple PowerShell tool calls in a single message.
    - If the commands depend on each other and must run sequentially, chain them in a single PowerShell call (see edition-specific chaining syntax above).
    - Use `;` only when you need to run commands sequentially but don't care if earlier commands fail.
    - DO NOT use newlines to separate commands (newlines are ok in quoted strings and here-strings)
  - Do NOT prefix commands with `cd` or `Set-Location` -- the working directory is already set to the correct project directory automatically.
  - Avoid unnecessary `Start-Sleep` commands:
    - Do not sleep between commands that can run immediately — just run them.
    - If your command is long running and you would like to be notified when it finishes — simply run your command using `run_in_background`. There is no need to sleep in this case.
    - Do not retry failing commands in a sleep loop — diagnose the root cause or consider an alternative approach.
    - If waiting for a background task you started with `run_in_background`, you will be notified when it completes — do not poll.
    - If you must poll an external process, use a check command rather than sleeping first.
    - If you must sleep, keep the duration short to avoid blocking the user.
  - For git commands:
    - Prefer to create a new commit rather than amending an existing commit.
    - Before running destructive operations (e.g., git reset --hard, git push --force, git checkout --), consider whether there is a safer alternative that achieves the same goal. Only use destructive operations when they are truly the best approach.
    - Never skip hooks (--no-verify) or bypass signing (--no-gpg-sign, -c commit.gpgsign=false) unless the user has explicitly asked for it. If a hook fails, investigate and fix the underlying issue.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: SendFeedback
tools.description:
Use this tool to draft feedback about Claude Code when you hit a high-signal moment. That includes both PRODUCT issues and MODEL-BEHAVIOR issues:
- a reproducible tool or product failure was just resolved or abandoned
- the user clearly expressed frustration with Claude Code or with how you handled the task
- you hit a missing capability that blocked a reasonable request
- you notice, or the user points out, that your own behavior in this session went wrong, for example: you gave a confident answer then had to retract it; you stopped short and handed work back when you could have finished; you declined or disputed a reasonable request; you spawned more subagents than the task warranted; your tone was off; you asked more clarifying questions than needed; you expanded scope beyond what was asked

The draft is QUEUED LOCALLY. It is never sent without the user's explicit approval, and calling this tool renders no UI and does not interrupt the conversation, so never announce it or ask the user about it mid-task.

Write `details` as short labeled bullets in this exact order, one to three lines each, no narrative paragraphs:
- **What happened:** the observed behavior vs. what was expected, with exact error text if short. Facts only.
- **What the user said:** the user's own words that prompted this, quoted. If nothing did, write "User didn't comment; observed by the model." Never paraphrase sentiment into a stronger claim.
- **Repro:** the minimal steps or shape that reproduces it.
- **Evidence:** identifiers a reader can chase, such as request IDs, timestamps, file paths, versions. Omit the bullet if there are none.

Constraints:
- Never fabricate or exaggerate user sentiment; report only what actually happened.
- Everything in the draft must be sourced from the user or the session, never inferred: leave unknown fields blank rather than guess, and add a final **Cause:** bullet only for a root cause you verified in-session.
- Use `area` to name the part of Claude Code the feedback is about (a feature, command, or workflow, e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing") when there is a clear one; leave it blank otherwise.
- Use `failure_mode` ONLY when the report is about model behavior (how Claude responded), not a product bug. Pick the single closest value, or `other` when it is a model-behavior issue that fits no listed value; omit the field only when the report is a product/tool bug with no model-behavior component.
- Use `task_category` to name what kind of task the session was doing, or `other` when it is a clear task that fits no listed value. Omit only if genuinely unclear.
- Do not include secrets or credentials. Refer to people by role ("a teammate", "the PR reviewer"), never by name, email address, or chat/user ID. This applies inside quoted user words too: replace a name or handle with a bracketed role (e.g. "[a teammate]") and keep the rest verbatim. Do not include customer-facing channel or DM IDs, or excerpts of customer content. Session, request, and run IDs, timestamps, repo/PR numbers, and file paths (written relative to the working directory, or ~-prefixed, not absolute paths under the user's home) remain the right evidence.
- If the issue looks like a security vulnerability: describe the class of problem, never a working exploit or step-by-step extraction path.
- Draft only at the natural moments listed above, and at most one draft per distinct issue; never re-draft the same issue in a session.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.

# Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge: Week 1 ("Touch Grass")

The page content is truncated, so details for the remaining partner categories are missing.

## Challenge Prompt and Theme
- **Core requirement:** Build a project where open-source AI is central. You may use an open-weight model, an open-source agent harness or framework, or local inference. The open components should make the project work.
- **Theme:** Projects that get people outdoors and reduce screen time, such as hiking, gardening, birding, run clubs, or fall foliage.
- **Example ideas:** An offline bird-call identifier, a frost-date garden planner, and a fall-foliage route builder for run clubs.
- **Writing requirement:** Explain why open innovation matters for your build, such as offline use, data privacy, fine-tuning, model swapping, or cost.
- **Bonus:** Use the project outdoors and report how it went.

## Key Dates
- Contest start: October 5, 2026
- Submissions due: October 11, 2026
- Winners announced: week of October 12

## Prizes
- **Overall winner:** $250 USD, DEV++ membership, and an exclusive winner badge
- **Each partner category winner:** $200 USD and an exclusive winner badge (the page says there are 16 partner categories)

## Partner Categories (visible on the page)
- **Best Use of Render:** Use Render as the AI runtime, to host an agent front end, or to run Hermes or OpenClaw.
- **Best Use of TabPFN (Prior Labs):** Use the tabular foundation model to forecast, predict, classify, or detect anomalies in historical data such as CSVs. It can be used inside an agent tool, with or without the MCP server, or on its own.
- **Best Use of Tinker (Thinking Machines):** Fine-tune a model for a specific task and show a clear gain in performance, latency, or cost over a baseline.
- **Qualcomm:** The category appears on the page, but its requirements are cut off.

The page also lists "Featured categories" for Render, but no other sponsor requirements are visible.

## Judging Criteria
1. Writing quality (weighted most heavily)
2. Relevance to the prompt and theme
3. Creativity
4. Technical execution
5. Use of partner technology (optional)

## Submission Requirements
- Publish on DEV using the submission template, tagged `devchallenge` and `hf26challenge`.
- Template sections: What I Built, Demo, Code, How I Built It, Why Does Open Innovation Matter?, My Agent Session (optional), and Prize Categories (list every category that applies).
- Demo: Share a deployed link or video.
- Code: Embed a GitHub repo.
- Agent session (optional but encouraged): Save it with DevRelay (devrelay.com) and embed it using the `agent_session` tag or link to it.
- Teams: One member publishes and credits teammates by listing their DEV usernames in the post body.

## Rules, Eligibility, and Notes
- The page does not state formal eligibility rules.
- Missed challenges can still be entered, since each challenge is a fresh start.
- The page is part of a five-challenge Hacktoberfest series. Hacktoberfest 2026 does not require pull requests.
- The page shows "Challenge Status: Live Ended," which is ambiguous. Check the DEV challenge hub for the current status.
- Partner credits (Tinker, Render, Backboard, ElevenLabs, and others) can be claimed at hacktoberfest.com/my/promos.

- **Requirement:** Use "Build with Copilot's coding agent, the Copilot CLI, or the new Copilot app." Also automate your project with GitHub Actions, or use Copilot to review contributors' PRs.
- **Prize:** $100 USD + exclusive winner badge

**Mastra**
- **Requirement:** "Orchestrate an agent over open models, add memory and tools to a chat agent." Alternatively, build a workflow that triages GitHub issues.
- **Prize:** $100 USD + exclusive winner badge

- **Requirement:** "Use Atlas as your data layer: Atlas Vector Search for retrieval, long-term memory for an agent." Also acceptable: the database behind an app built on an open-weight model.
- **Prize:** $100 USD + exclusive winner badge

**Sentry Agent Tracing**
- **Requirement:** "Show your agent's work: how it's set up, how it performs (latency, tokens, cost), what you found." Include traces or screenshots in your write-up.
- **Prize:** $100 USD + exclusive winner badge

**SerpApi**
- **Requirement:** Give an agent live web search, ground a RAG app in fresh results, or track news for an open-source project.
- **Prize:** $100 USD + exclusive winner badge

Context: Theme = build a project where open-source AI (open-weight model, open-source agent framework, or local inference) is central AND that gets people outdoors and reduces screen time (hiking, gardening, birding, run clubs, fall foliage). Investigate:
1. Saturation: count/estimate existing #hf26challenge submissions on dev.to (dev.to/t/hf26challenge, and the dev.to API https://dev.to/api/articles?tag=hf26challenge) and which partner categories each claims. Identify which categories have zero or very few entries. Also check past DEV challenges for which sponsor categories historically get few entries (hardware, unfamiliar/new sponsors such as TabPFN, Tinker, Entire, Backboard, Tiger Data, Temporal).
2. Newness and unfamiliarity: which sponsors/products are newest or least known (TabPFN-2.5/TabPFN MCP, Tinker API, Entire, Backboard R-CLI, Tiger Data/Tiger MCP), and what their current docs, APIs, free credits, and quickstarts look like, so a build is feasible in ~1 day.
3. Hot topics: verified trending topics in Oct 2026 that fit the outdoor theme (e.g., fall foliage peak forecasts, bird migration/BirdCast, frost dates, air quality/wildfire smoke, trail conditions, citizen science like iNaturalist/eBird, local/offline AI, small open models).
4. Strategy: recommend the single best under-saturated category (or stack of 2-4 low-competition categories that one project can credibly claim), with a concrete project idea that is feasible to build and write up in about 24 hours. Include the data sources/APIs, the open model, the architecture, and a write-up angle that maximizes the writing-quality score.

Output: a ranked table of categories by estimated competition, then the recommended idea with build plan and sources.

content.text:
The research is done: 104 agents ran, and each claim was checked by 3 votes.

## The short answer

**Don't enter Gemma.** It appears in about 186 of the ~1,160 Touch Grass posts. The $200 categories with almost no competition are **Arduino, DigitalOcean and Tinker**.

Counts are sponsor names found in post titles, descriptions and tags on Oct 10:

| Rank | Category | Prize | Mentions | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Arduino UNO Q | $200 | 0 | Only if you already own the board |
| 2 | DigitalOcean | $200 | 1 | Fallback main target |
| 3 | **Tinker** | **$200** | **2** | **Best main target. Cloud fine-tuning, so no GPU needed on your side** |
| 4 | SerpApi / Mastra | $100 | 1 each | |
| 5 | **Temporal / Entire** / Sentry / Backboard | $100 | 2 each | **Temporal and Entire have the cheapest setup** |
| 6 | Tiger Data / MongoDB | $100 | 3 each | |
| 7 | Render / Copilot / ElevenLabs | $100–200 | 5–6 | |
| 8 | TabPFN | $200 | 17 | Frost and leaf-peeping projects are already entered |
| 9 | Gemma | $200 | 186 | Use the model if you like, but don't enter the category |

**Caveats:**
- These counts probably undercount, because they don't read the "Prize Categories" section inside each post.
- Around 150–200 new posts arrive each day, and a last-day surge is likely.
- In the previous challenge every category got a winner, so none will be completely empty.
- **You can enter many categories but win only one.** Entering more raises your odds, not your payout.

## Strategy: Tinker ($200) as the main target, plus Temporal and Entire ($100 each)

- **Tinker:** Thinking Machines' cloud fine-tuning API. You write the training loop on your laptop and they run the GPUs. The category requires a measurable gain over a baseline, and that requirement is exactly what most people skip.
- **Entire:** almost free to add. Install their CLI in your repo **before you start coding** so it records your agent sessions, then link those sessions in the write-up.
- **Temporal:** an official durable-AI-agent tutorial gives you starter code. It calls the model through LiteLLM, so you can point it at your open model.

## The idea, adjusted for what's already entered

The research suggested a "should I go outside?" agent, but **that already exists**: GrassCast is an entry, and FloraQuest has already entered Tinker. Here is a different version that keeps the same category stack:

### 🥾 TrailTruth: park alerts become one go/no-go trail card

- **Problem:** National park alerts are walls of text, such as closure notices, bear activity and washouts. People skim them, or never see them, and then drive to a closed trailhead.
- **Data:** the free NPS API (`developer.nps.gov`, `/alerts`). Each alert already carries a category (Danger, Caution, Park Closure, Information), so you get **real labels without labeling anything yourself**.
- **Tinker part:** fine-tune a small open model (Llama or Qwen, 1–8B) on Tinker. It turns each raw alert into strict JSON: `{trail, hazard_type, severity, closed: bool, go/no-go}`. Report **base model vs fine-tuned** on held-out alerts: JSON-valid rate, category accuracy and closure accuracy. That table is your "clear gain."
- **Temporal part:** a weekly workflow fetches alerts for your saved parks, runs the model, and outputs one printable card. Retries handle a flaky API. In the demo, kill the worker mid-run and show it resuming.
- **Theme fit:** you check the card once and then go outside. That's the screen-time angle for the write-up, and it also covers the bonus: take the card on a real hike and report how it went.
- **Why open innovation matters:** a small fine-tuned model is cheap, can run offline at the trailhead, and keeps the parks you visit private.

### Rough 24-hour plan
1. **1 hour:** install Entire and scaffold from Temporal's durable-agent / LiteLLM example.
2. **3 hours:** pull about 500 NPS alerts, split train/test, and run the baseline evaluation.
3. **3 hours:** train the LoRA on Tinker and evaluate again.
4. **4 hours:** build the workflow (fetch, classify, render the card) and record the crash-and-resume demo.
5. **2 hours:** deploy and record a GIF.
6. **4–5 hours:** write it up, since writing carries the most judging weight. Lead with a story, then the results table, the demo, and the Entire session links.

## Not verified by the research
- Tinker's pricing and free credits. A third party reports $150, but that's unconfirmed. Claim whatever credits apply at hacktoberfest.com/my/promos first. If Tinker is blocked, switch the main target to **DigitalOcean** and serve the model on a GPU Droplet.
- NPS API details. It's free and long-standing, but I didn't confirm the current schema. Check that first.
- Pointing Temporal's starter code at a local model is inferred from LiteLLM's support, not demonstrated.
- No outdoor topics were confirmed as trending this month.

The deadline is **Oct 11, 11:59 PM PDT**. Do you want me to scaffold TrailTruth here in `GRASS`?

content.content:
**What it is:** BoardUI is a React design system for dashboards and agentic interfaces. It includes 85 components (19 of them data charts), 10 Pro templates, and 400+ design tokens, and it was designed in Figma. It's built on React 19.2, Tailwind CSS v4, React Aria, and TanStack Table. It's both a component library and a design kit.

**Installation:**
- **CLI:** The page shows the command as `npm boardui@latest add button-group`, which adds a component to your project. Installation is handled through the CLI.
- **MCP for AI agents:** Connect with `npx -y boardui@latest mcp`, which the page's Cursor and VS Code links use. Claude Code and Codex are also supported.
- **Shadcn registry or copy-paste:** The page doesn't mention either.
- **Free tier:** The free components are in a public GitHub repo (github.com/BoardUI/boardui) under the MIT license.

**Components (examples):** Composer attachments, Web search, Agent limits, Data table, Sidebar, Agent progress, Composer loader, Agent thinking, Calendar, Auth card, Meeting schedule, Charts, File upload, and Contributor profile. Charts include Funnel, Earnings, Radar, Sankey, Radial, Area, and Combo. Several charts and templates are Pro-only.

**Templates:** Dashboard, Project board, Marketing, Calendar, Finance, Medical Report, AI Chat, AI Image Generation, and Profile.

**URL patterns:**
- Component listing: `/components`
- Single component: `/components/<slug>` (e.g., `/components/data-table`)
- Variants or sections: `/components/<slug>#<anchor>` (e.g., `/components/radar-chart-card#variants`)
- Templates: `/templates/<slug>` (e.g., `/templates/ai-chat`)
- Docs and install: `/getting-started` and `/installation`
- MCP guide: `/mcp`
- Pricing: `/#pricing`

content.content:
**Prerequisites**
- React 19 and Tailwind CSS v4. The page says any setup with both works.
- Next.js is the documented example. The page also has guides for Vite, React Router, and Astro, but their specific steps aren't in the content provided.

**1. Create a project (optional)**

```
npx create-next-app@latest my-app
```

Accept the defaults: TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, and the `@/*` import alias.

**2. Run init in the project root**

```
npx boardui@latest init
```

This installs `react-aria-components`, `tailwind-merge`, and `@remixicon/react`. It writes the `styles/` and `utils/` folders, including the theme, typography, global styles, and the `cx` utility. It also prints the import line to add. The page also offers pnpm and yarn versions of this command.

**3. Import the stylesheet in your root layout**

In `app/layout.tsx`:

```tsx
import "@/styles/globals.css";
```

This replaces the default `"./globals.css"` import.

**4. Add components**

```
npx boardui@latest add button select date-picker
```

Internal dependencies and npm packages resolve automatically. Use the component names separated by spaces.

**Tokens and fonts**
- `styles/theme.css` holds the design tokens (colors, typography, radii, shadows). The manual route creates this file yourself.
- Fonts: Inter is loaded with `next/font` in `app/layout.tsx` and exposed as `--font-inter`. The monospace font, JetBrains Mono, is exposed as `--font-mono-source`. The page doesn't show the `next/font` code itself.

input.content:
# TrailTruth — shared build contract

> National-park alerts → one go/no-go trail card. Check once, then go outside.

Hackathon: DEV "Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge — Week 1: Touch Grass".
Deadline **2026-10-11 23:59 PDT**. Target categories: **Tinker** (main, $200), **Temporal**, **Entire**, optionally **Render** / **Sentry**.

## Story in one paragraph
NPS publishes ~600 live alerts (`https://developer.nps.gov/api/v1/alerts`, `api_key=DEMO_KEY` works) — barred owls dive-bombing hikers, volcano closures, washed-out bridges. They're walls of text. We **distill a big open-weight model into a tiny one with Tinker**: a large open model labels every alert into strict JSON (teacher), then we LoRA-fine-tune a 1–3B open model (student) on Tinker. We show base-student vs LoRA-student vs teacher on held-out alerts (JSON-valid rate, decision accuracy, closure F1, latency, cost). A **Temporal** workflow runs weekly: fetch alerts for your saved parks → classify (retries on flaky API/model) → render ONE printable trail card. Then the app shuts up. KPI: minutes *not* spent in the app.

## Repo layout (each owner touches only their dir)
```
data/            raw + labeled alerts, train/test splits          (ML agent)
ml/              python: fetch, teacher label, train_tinker, eval  (ML agent)
ml/results/      eval.json, predictions.jsonl, charts              (ML agent)
agent/           python: Temporal workflows/activities/worker + FastAPI  (Backend agent)
web/             Next.js 16 + BoardUI dashboard                    (UI agent)
docs/            DEV post draft, screenshots                       (Writer agent)
shared/schema.py canonical schema (do not change without updating web/lib/types.ts)
```

## Canonical model output — `TrailVerdict`
The model receives `title` + `description` (+ `category` NOT given to the model; it is a held-out label) and must emit exactly this JSON:
```json
{
  "hazard_type": "closure|wildlife|weather|fire|water|geologic|construction|air_quality|road|facility|other",
  "severity": 1,                    // 1 = info, 2 = caution, 3 = danger
  "trails_affected": ["Bluff Trail"],
  "is_closed": false,
  "decision": "go|caution|no_go",
  "reason": "Territorial barred owl on Bluff Trail section; stay alert."   // <= 20 words
}
```
Ground truth: NPS `category` (Danger / Caution / Park Closure / Information) is a *real* human label → maps to expected decision:
`Information→go`, `Caution→caution`, `Danger→no_go`, `Park Closure→no_go` (if the closure affects trails/areas) — teacher labels fill hazard_type/trails/reason.

## Processed alert record (what backend serves, what UI renders) — `ProcessedAlert`
```json
{
  "id": "6822FAF9-...", "park_code": "chch", "park_name": "Chickamauga & Chattanooga NMP",
  "title": "...", "description": "...", "url": "", "nps_category": "Caution",
  "last_indexed": "2026-10-09",
  "verdict": { TrailVerdict },
  "model": "llama-3.2-1b-trailtruth-lora", "latency_ms": 212
}
```

## TrailCard — the one thing the user takes outside
```json
{
  "id": "card_2026-10-11_chch-havo", "generated_at": "ISO", "week_of": "2026-10-11",
  "parks": [ { "park_code": "havo", "park_name": "...", "decision": "go|caution|no_go",
               "headline": "Go — but skip Halemaʻumaʻu Trail", "closed_trails": ["..."],
               "watch_for": ["..."], "alert_ids": ["..."] } ],
  "overall": "go|caution|no_go", "workflow_id": "trailcard-...", "model": "..."
}
```

## Backend API (FastAPI, `http://localhost:8000`)
- `GET  /api/health`
- `GET  /api/parks` → `[{park_code, park_name, states, alert_count, worst_decision}]`
- `GET  /api/alerts?park=havo` → `ProcessedAlert[]`
- `POST /api/cards` body `{parks: ["havo","chch"]}` → starts Temporal workflow, returns `{workflow_id}`
- `GET  /api/cards/{workflow_id}` → `{status, card?: TrailCard, steps: [{name, status, attempt, started_at, ended_at, error?}]}`
- `GET  /api/runs` → recent workflow runs (same shape, no card)
- `GET  /api/eval` → contents of `ml/results/eval.json`

## `ml/results/eval.json`
```json
{
  "test_size": 120, "generated_at": "ISO",
  "models": [
    {"name": "teacher (Qwen3-235B)", "role": "teacher", "json_valid": 0.99, "decision_acc": 0.9, "closure_f1": 0.9, "hazard_acc": 0.8, "p50_latency_ms": 1800, "cost_per_1k_alerts_usd": 0.9},
    {"name": "Llama-3.2-1B base", "role": "base", ...},
    {"name": "Llama-3.2-1B + TrailTruth LoRA", "role": "lora", ...}
  ],
  "confusion": {"lora": {"labels": ["go","caution","no_go"], "matrix": [[..]]}},
  "training": {"steps": 0, "epochs": 0, "lora_rank": 32, "loss_curve": [[step, loss], ...]},
  "examples": [{"title": "...", "base_output": "...", "lora_output": "...", "expected_decision": "..."}]
}
```

## Model providers (pluggable, env `TRAILTRUTH_MODEL_PROVIDER`)
- `tinker` — Tinker SamplingClient on saved LoRA weights (`TINKER_API_KEY`, `TRAILTRUTH_TINKER_MODEL_PATH`)
- `openai` — any OpenAI-compatible local server (Ollama / llama.cpp / vLLM) via `TRAILTRUTH_BASE_URL`, `TRAILTRUTH_MODEL`
- `heuristic` — deterministic keyword fallback so everything runs with zero keys (dev/demo only; clearly labeled)

## Fixtures
Until real results exist, everyone codes against `shared/fixtures/*.json` (written by the backend agent from real NPS data + heuristic verdicts). The UI must render from `web/public/fixtures/` when the API is down (static demo deploy).

NPS publishes ~600 live alerts (`https://developer.nps.gov/api/v1/alerts`, `api_key=DEMO_KEY` works) — barred owls dive-bombing hikers, volcano closures, washed-out bridges. They're walls of text. We **distill a big open-weight model into a tiny one with Tinker**: a large open model labels every alert into strict JSON (teacher), then we LoRA-fine-tune a 1–3B open model (student) on Tinker. We show base-student vs LoRA-student vs teacher on held-out alerts (JSON-valid rate, decision accuracy, closure F1, latency, cost). A **Temporal** workflow runs weekly: fetch alerts for your saved parks → classify (retries on flaky API/model) → render ONE printable trail card. Then the app shuts up. KPI: minutes *not* spent in the app.

## Repo layout (each owner touches only their dir)
```
data/            raw + labeled alerts, train/test splits          (ML agent)
ml/              python: fetch, teacher label, train_tinker, eval  (ML agent)
ml/results/      eval.json, predictions.jsonl, charts              (ML agent)
agent/           python: Temporal workflows/activities/worker + FastAPI  (Backend agent)
web/             Next.js 16 + BoardUI dashboard                    (UI agent)
docs/            DEV post draft, screenshots                       (Writer agent)
shared/schema.py canonical schema (do not change without updating web/lib/types.ts)
```

## Canonical model output — `TrailVerdict`
The model receives `title` + `description` (+ `category` NOT given to the model; it is a held-out label) and must emit exactly this JSON:
```json
{
  "hazard_type": "closure|wildlife|weather|fire|water|geologic|construction|air_quality|road|facility|other",
  "severity": 1,                    // 1 = info, 2 = caution, 3 = danger
  "trails_affected": ["Bluff Trail"],
  "is_closed": false,
  "decision": "go|caution|no_go",
  "reason": "Territorial barred owl on Bluff Trail section; stay alert."   // <= 20 words
}
```
Ground truth: NPS `category` (Danger / Caution / Park Closure / Information) is a *real* human label → maps to expected decision:
`Information→go`, `Caution→caution`, `Danger→no_go`, `Park Closure→no_go` (if the closure affects trails/areas) — teacher labels fill hazard_type/trails/reason.

## Processed alert record (what backend serves, what UI renders) — `ProcessedAlert`
```json
{
  "id": "6822FAF9-...", "park_code": "chch", "park_name": "Chickamauga & Chattanooga NMP",
  "title": "...", "description": "...", "url": "", "nps_category": "Caution",
  "last_indexed": "2026-10-09",
  "verdict": { TrailVerdict },
  "model": "llama-3.2-1b-trailtruth-lora", "latency_ms": 212
}
```

## TrailCard — the one thing the user takes outside
```json
{
  "id": "card_2026-10-11_chch-havo", "generated_at": "ISO", "week_of": "2026-10-11",
  "parks": [ { "park_code": "havo", "park_name": "...", "decision": "go|caution|no_go",
               "headline": "Go — but skip Halemaʻumaʻu Trail", "closed_trails": ["..."],
               "watch_for": ["..."], "alert_ids": ["..."] } ],
  "overall": "go|caution|no_go", "workflow_id": "trailcard-...", "model": "..."
}
```

## Backend API (FastAPI, `http://localhost:8000`)
- `GET  /api/health`
- `GET  /api/parks` → `[{park_code, park_name, states, alert_count, worst_decision}]`
- `GET  /api/alerts?park=havo` → `ProcessedAlert[]`
- `POST /api/cards` body `{parks: ["havo","chch"]}` → starts Temporal workflow, returns `{workflow_id}`
- `GET  /api/cards/{workflow_id}` → `{status, card?: TrailCard, steps: [{name, status, attempt, started_at, ended_at, error?}]}`
- `GET  /api/runs` → recent workflow runs (same shape, no card)
- `GET  /api/eval` → contents of `ml/results/eval.json`

```json
{
  "test_size": 120, "generated_at": "ISO",
  "models": [
    {"name": "teacher (Qwen3-235B)", "role": "teacher", "json_valid": 0.99, "decision_acc": 0.9, "closure_f1": 0.9, "hazard_acc": 0.8, "p50_latency_ms": 1800, "cost_per_1k_alerts_usd": 0.9},
    {"name": "Llama-3.2-1B base", "role": "base", ...},
    {"name": "Llama-3.2-1B + TrailTruth LoRA", "role": "lora", ...}
  ],
  "confusion": {"lora": {"labels": ["go","caution","no_go"], "matrix": [[..]]}},
  "training": {"steps": 0, "epochs": 0, "lora_rank": 32, "loss_curve": [[step, loss], ...]},
  "examples": [{"title": "...", "base_output": "...", "lora_output": "...", "expected_decision": "..."}]
}
```

## Model providers (pluggable, env `TRAILTRUTH_MODEL_PROVIDER`)
- `tinker` — Tinker SamplingClient on saved LoRA weights (`TINKER_API_KEY`, `TRAILTRUTH_TINKER_MODEL_PATH`)

"""Canonical TrailTruth schema. Mirror any change in web/lib/types.ts."""
from __future__ import annotations

from typing import Literal

from pydantic import BaseModel, Field

HazardType = Literal[
    "closure", "wildlife", "weather", "fire", "water", "geologic",
    "construction", "air_quality", "road", "facility", "other",
]
Decision = Literal["go", "caution", "no_go"]
NpsCategory = Literal["Danger", "Caution", "Park Closure", "Information"]

CATEGORY_TO_DECISION: dict[str, Decision] = {
    "Information": "go",
    "Caution": "caution",
    "Danger": "no_go",
    "Park Closure": "no_go",
}


class TrailVerdict(BaseModel):
    hazard_type: HazardType
    severity: int = Field(ge=1, le=3)
    trails_affected: list[str] = Field(default_factory=list)
    is_closed: bool
    decision: Decision
    reason: str = Field(max_length=200)


class ProcessedAlert(BaseModel):
    id: str
    park_code: str
    park_name: str = ""
    title: str
    description: str
    url: str = ""
    nps_category: str
    last_indexed: str = ""
    verdict: TrailVerdict
    model: str
    latency_ms: int = 0


class CardPark(BaseModel):
    park_code: str
    park_name: str
    decision: Decision
    headline: str
    closed_trails: list[str] = Field(default_factory=list)
    watch_for: list[str] = Field(default_factory=list)
    alert_ids: list[str] = Field(default_factory=list)


class TrailCard(BaseModel):
    id: str
    generated_at: str
    week_of: str
    parks: list[CardPark]
    overall: Decision
    workflow_id: str
    model: str


SYSTEM_PROMPT = (
    "You are TrailTruth. Read one U.S. National Park Service alert and reply with ONLY a JSON object, "
    "no prose, with keys: hazard_type (one of closure, wildlife, weather, fire, water, geologic, construction, "
    "air_quality, road, facility, other), severity (1 info, 2 caution, 3 danger), trails_affected (list of trail "
    "or area names, may be empty), is_closed (true if any trail/area/road is closed), decision (go, caution, no_go "
    "for a hiker planning a visit to the affected area), reason (<= 20 words)."
)


def user_prompt(title: str, description: str) -> str:
    return f"ALERT TITLE: {title}\nALERT TEXT: {description}"

Stack (required): Next.js (latest, App Router, TypeScript, Tailwind v4) + **BoardUI** (https://boardui.com — React design system for dashboards & agentic interfaces, MIT free tier at github.com/BoardUI/boardui, built on React Aria + Tailwind v4 + TanStack Table + Remix Icons). Setup: `npx create-next-app@latest web --ts --tailwind --app --eslint --use-npm --yes` (non-interactive; check flags), then in web/: `npx boardui@latest init`, import `@/styles/globals.css` in app/layout.tsx, `npx boardui@latest add <components>` (browse https://boardui.com/components to pick: sidebar, data-table, charts (area/radial/bar — free ones), badge, button, select, tabs, agent-progress, agent-thinking, calendar, etc.). If the boardui CLI is blocked, clone/copy components from the MIT GitHub repo. Use BoardUI's tokens (styles/theme.css) and extend them with a custom outdoor palette. Inter + JetBrains Mono per BoardUI docs.

Design research FIRST (15 min max): look at Dribbble / Framer / Mobbin-style references via WebSearch/WebFetch for "national park app UI", "trail map dashboard", "outdoor weather dashboard dribbble", "Linear-style dashboard", "topographic UI". Write 5–8 bullet design principles you took from them into `web/DESIGN.md` (with reference URLs). Aesthetic direction: **"NPS ranger signage meets Linear-grade enterprise dashboard"** — calm, dense, typographic, earth palette (forest/pine green, granite, sandstone, sky; signal colors go=green, caution=amber, no_go=red with color-blind-safe icons/shapes too), subtle topographic contour-line SVG textures, light + dark mode, impeccable spacing, keyboard focus states, responsive down to phone width (16px gutters, no horizontal scroll).

Pages (App Router):
1. `/` Overview — hero statement ("Check once. Then go outside."), watchlist of parks (add/remove via select, persisted in localStorage with try/catch), per-park decision badge, counts by decision, "Generate this week's card" button (POST /api/cards → poll /api/cards/{id}; show BoardUI agent-progress style step timeline with attempt counts/retries).
2. `/card` — **the hero artifact**: a beautifully typeset, PRINTABLE trail card (print CSS: @media print → single sheet, black-on-white, QR to source alert URLs optional), also "Save to lock screen" (export as PNG via html-to-image or canvas). Big decision per park, closed trails, what to watch for. This is what goes in the DEV post cover image — make it gorgeous.
3. `/alerts` — enterprise data table (BoardUI data-table/TanStack): filter by park, decision, hazard_type, NPS category; row expand shows original alert text vs model JSON verdict side-by-side, latency, model name.
4. `/lab` — Model Lab: base vs LoRA vs teacher vs heuristic metrics from /api/eval (bar/radial charts: json_valid, decision_acc, closure_f1, hazard_acc, latency, cost per 1k), loss curve area chart, confusion matrix grid, side-by-side example outputs. Show a "pending — awaiting training run" state elegantly when `pending: true`.
5. `/runs` — Temporal workflow runs: list + detail timeline with retries highlighted (attempt 2 after NPS 503), "resumed after worker crash" event.

Quality bar: run `npm run build` with zero errors and zero type errors; run `npm run dev` and screenshot each page (use Playwright via `npx playwright` if available — install chromium if allowed; else skip screenshots) into `docs/screenshots/` (you may create that dir) at 1440px and 390px widths, light and dark. Review your own screenshots critically and fix anything that looks amateur (alignment, empty states, contrast, overflow). Do not git commit. Final report (<300 words): pages built, BoardUI components used, how to run, screenshot paths, known gaps.
